sektioner.rubrik: Sustainability PolicyThe Sustainability Policy sets out Ericssons
sektioner.text: overarching principles for environmental sustainability and emphasizes the use of life-cycle analysis to identify signicant environmental aspects and assess the impacts of ICT. This approach supports continuous reduction of negative environmental impacts across operations. The policy also addresses sustainability requirements in the supply chain and aims to strengthen employees awareness and understanding of sustainability. Business and Human Rights StatementThe Business and Human Rights Statement outlines Ericssons commitment to respecting internationally recognized human rights, including those set out in the United Nations International Bill of Human Rights and the International Labour Organizations Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work. Ericsson strives to implement the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights across its operations and conducts human rights due diligence to identify, assess and mitigate salient risks. The statement also addresses access to grievance mechanisms and remedy, as well as engagement with employees and stakeholders to support continuous improvement.Sustainability criteria in variable incentive schemesSustainability-related performance criteria have been included in the 2025 share-based long-term variable compensation for the Executive Team and their direct reports. 5% of the performance criteria is based on annual reductions in GHG emissions (Scope 1, Scope 2 and Business Travel within Scope 3), in line with the Companys trajectory toward its 2030 emissions reduction target. Another 5% is based on increasing the percentage of women in leadership roles through merit-based people management, in compliance with all applicable anti-discrimination laws. Further details of the long-term variable compensation program are described in note G3 to the consolidated nancial statements.Ericsson also provides short-term cash-based incentive plans for selected employees. These plans link variable compensation to both performance and ethical conduct. For top management, a portion of the payout is also tied to predened integrity criteria related to compliance, security and the work environment. Underperformance against these criteria may reduce or, in consecutive years, fully cancel the payout. If an employee is found to have breached the Code of Business Ethics, the Company may reduce, withhold, or reclaim such compensation in line with its internal sanction process and applicable legal requirements. The Remuneration Committee reviews and prepares for resolution by the Board proposals to the Annual General Meeting on the long-term variable compensation program and similar equity arrangements. The Remuneration Committee also approves target levels of short-term variable compensation for the Executive Team, excluding the President and CEO. Non-executive members of the Board of Directors do not receive variable or perforFurther details on Ericssons remuneration practices are provided in the Remuneration Report.Risk management and internal control over sustainability reportingEricsson applies a structured risk management approach to its sustainability reporting process. Reporting risks across the Sustainability Statement are assessed using a framework that considers information complexity, data source reliability, value-chain dependencies, stakeholder sensitivity and process maturity.Areas with elevated reporting risk typically include disclosures based on multiple data systems or external information, as well as those requiring complex estimations. These risks are mitigated through documented methodologies, gradual system integration, automated consolidation where possible and engagement with key data providers to support accuracy and consistency.Reporting and accounting policies are in place for all key sustainability areas. Dedicated reporting software now supports most numerical disclosures through standardized data collection and automated consolidation, with remaining metrics to be integrated going forward. Internal controls include four-eye reviews, analytical procedures to detect deviations and completeness checks prior to consolidation. sektioner.rubrik: Scope 3 upstream, transportation and product end-of-life emissionsMost
sektioner.text: planned upstream emission reductions focus on lowering embodied carbon emissions in Ericssons product portfolio. Key measures include lightweight product design, alternative material choices, increased supplier use of renewable energy and improved transport efciency. Supplier engagement will prioritize those contributing most to Ericssons supply-chain emissions, such as aluminum die-casting, and the manufacturing of printed circuit boards and integrated circuits.Business travel emissions are expected to increase from the 2020 baseline, which was affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, but are not expected to exceed 50% of pre-pandemic levels. The planned measures are expected to contribute to a net reduction of annual Scope 3 upstream, transportation and product end-of-life GHG emissions by approximately 1.3 million metric tons, or 50%, by 2030.Scope 3 downstream emissions from the use of sold productsEricsson relies on three main levers to reduce indirect downstream emissions from the use of its products. The size of these levers has been estimated based on projected sales and forecasted energy consumption of hardware and software.The rst and most signicant lever within Ericssons direct control is improving the energy performance of hardware, software and service solutions. A key progress indicator is the target to reduce the average energy consumption of typical radio base station sites. Ericsson is also providing guidance to customers on planning, building and operating energy-optimized networks. This lever is expected to reduce annual GHG emissions by approximately 8.6 million metric tons by The second lever involves supporting customers transition to renewable electricity. While Ericsson cannot directly inuence electricity purchasing decisions, the Company facilitates this shift by enabling integration of on-site renewable solutions, such as solar and wind power, at base station sites. Ericssons transition plan assumes a conservative estimate of approximately 50% renewable electricity use by customers in 2030, which is lower than projections from the Global System for Mobile Communications Association (GSMA). This lever is expected to reduce annual emissions by approximately 5.1 million metric tons.The third lever is the expected growth of fossil-free energy in national electricity grids powering mobile networks. This depends on external factors, including national energy policies, and is therefore subject to high uncertainty. Depending on the scenario, this lever could contribute to annual emission reductions ranging from zero to 6.3 million metric tons. Together, these levers are expected to contribute to a net reduction of annual Scope 3 downstream GHG emissions from the use of sold products by between 13.7 and 20.0 million metric tons, or 50% to 73%, by 2030.Financial resources allocated to the transition plan Climate-related actions and initiatives are embedded in Ericssons ongoing operations and business planning. Emission-reduction measures within own operations do not currently incur material capital or operating expenditures warranting separate disclosure. The largest emission source, downstream emissions from the use of sold products, is addressed primarily through improved product energy performance driven by R&D activities and through customer actions such as the use of renewable electricity.Part of Ericssons R&D investments to enhance the energy performance of existing and future products is nanced through green bonds. In 2023, Ericsson issued its inaugural EUR 500 million green bond under its Green Financing Framework, and by the end of 2024 all proceeds had been allocated to hardware and software R&D to support Ericssons goal to reduce the energy consumption of typical radio base station sites. Total R&D expenditure is disclosed on page 14 of the Board of Directors Report.The Companys activities are not, to any signicant extent, covered by the delegated regulations on climate change mitigation or adaptation under the EU taxonomy. Accordingly, no material investments are currently planned to align with the taxonomy criteria for these environmental objectives.Locked-in emissionsCumulative locked-in GHG emissions from Ericssons own operations are not considered material, as Ericsson does not operate any emission-intensive assets. Locked-in emissions from the use phase of sold products depend on the electricity required to power customer networks, and therefore on customers energy sourcing choices. sektioner.rubrik: Most electronic components contain small amounts of substances
sektioner.text: of concern, and in some cases substances of very high concern. These substances are used during manufacturing and are therefore embedded in the nished products that Ericsson sells. If not properly managed or disposed of at end-of-life, these substances can leak into the environment and harm ecosystems and human These are potential negative impacts of a systemic nature, occurring mainly upstream in Ericssons value chain, where such substances are used in component manufacturing, and downstream when products are not properly recycled. Ericssons own operations primarily involve the assembly of components and therefore do not involve the addition of signicant volumes of these substances. The exposure to these impacts is current, but their magnitude is expected to decline over the medium to long term, assuming Ericsson continues to phase out some of these substances from its products. While not identied as material risks in the materiality assessment, regulatory developments, such as proposals to restrict the use of PFAS in the European Union, represent emerging issues that Ericsson monitors and integrates into its strategy from a precautionary perspective. Depending on the nal requirements, such developments could in the long term lead to higher compliance costs, additional research and development needs or constraints in the availability of alternative materials.Policies In addition to Ericssons Code of Conduct for Business Partners, suppliers with signicant environmental impact such as manufacturing service providers, shipping and logistics companies and network rollout partners, must meet additional environmental requirements. These include compliance with Ericssons Lists of Banned and Restricted Substances, which identify substances that are restricted for use in products or in the production of purchased components. This requirement also applies to substances used in batteries and packaging. The structure and classication of substances follow the Material Declaration for Products of and for the Electrotechnical Industry standard, IEC 62474, and include additional substances dened by Ericsson. Banned and restricted substances may not be intentionally added in specied applications, and substitution of substances under observation is recommended as a precautionary measure. Further information about the Code of Conduct for Business Partners is included General disclosureManagement actions Material declarationsTo monitor substances in purchased components and equipment, Ericsson collects material declarations from suppliers. Upon request, suppliers must declare the full material content, including substances on the REACH candidate list and certain raw materials dened in the EU Critical Raw Materials List. A SCIP reporting process is in place to meet reporting requirements of the EU Waste Framework Directive. Ericsson collaborates with hardware suppliers and encourages proactive substitution of substances under observation where feasible.Management of electronic wasteTo meet extended producer responsibilities for electrical and electronic equipment, Ericsson offers collection of end-of-life products to its customers through its e-Waste Management Program. The program helps reduce the risk of hazardous substances in products being disposed of in ways that could cause pollution. Further information is proResource use and circular economyEnvironmental Management SystemEricssons environmental management system is certied to the ISO 14001:2015 standard and covers management, research, product management, development, supply, sales, installation and maintenance of hardware, software, services and solutions for ICT. It is integrated into the Ericsson Group Management System and includes processes for audits, assessments and management reviews. Environmental regulations are regularly monitored at country level to support local compliance. An environmental risk management framework is in place, aligned with Ericssons overall ERM framework. Employees shall report environmental incidents through the Companys incident reporting system, and suppliers are required to do the same as set out in the Code of Conduct for Business Partners. Regulatory monitoringIn 2025, Ericsson continued to monitor substance-related regulatory developments, such as PFAS, in the markets where it operates to assess potential implications for its business and the telecommunications sector.TargetsEricsson has not set targets for its material pollution-related impacts but continues to assess whether target setting would be appropriate as part of its management approach. The effectiveness of Ericssons policies and actions in these areas is, in part, monitored through the collection of material declarations from its suppliers.Emissions to air from own operations Although not linked to any material impacts, risks or opportunities, emissions of air pollutants from Ericssons operations are disclosed in Appendix 5, as this information is frequently requested by external stakeholders. These emissions mainly arise from fossil fuel combustion in the service vehicle eet and from local heating at facilities. Most of Ericssons own manufacturing sites are not within the scope of regulations related to air pollutants, such as the European Unions Emissions Trading Scheme, the Industrial Emissions Directive or the European Pollutant Release and Transfer Register. Ericsson complies with all applicable local regulations on the control and monitoring of emissions to air. sektioner.text: subtopicImpact, risk or opportunityTypeImpact occursResource inows and outowsMetals and minerals used in electronics manufacturingActual negative impactUpstream, own operationsWasteGeneration of electronic wasteActual negative impactUpstream, own operations, downstreamResource use and circular economyAs part of its materiality assessment, Ericsson evaluated its impacts on biodiversity and ecosystems. The key drivers of biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation linked to Ericssons direct and indirect activities are climate change, use of natural resources and pollution. These impacts, along with Ericssons approach to managing them, are addressed in other sections of the Sustainability Statement.Other drivers, such as land- and sea- use change, land degradation, desertication, and invasive species, were not identied as material in Ericssons value chain. Ericssons own facilities are located in urban or semi-urban areas, with limited impact on land use and surrounding ecosystems. The Company supports customers in the installation of telecommunication networks and network sites. When planning these installations, standard procedures are applied to minimize environmental impacts, including site location planning to reduce land-use effects.Ericsson addresses biodiversity-related impacts primarily through actions to mitigate climate change, reduce pollution and transition to a more circular business model. Biodiversity and ecosystems are therefore not currently managed or reported on as a standalone topic.Resource inows and outowsProducing hardware for mobile networks requires metals and minerals such as iron, aluminum, copper and, even though in smaller volumes, rare earth elements and other raw materials. Extracting and processing these nite resources causes negative environmental impacts and contributes to the scarcity and depletion of global resources. These actual negative impacts are current and expected to persist over the medium to long term. They are concentrated upstream in the value chain, where mining and rening take place. Although many metals like aluminum and copper are widely recycled, rare earth elements and some other raw materials have low recycling rates and limited substitutes, which sustains the need for primary extraction. Ericsson does not process raw materials in its own operations and mainly assembles components, but can inuence material efciency, recyclability, product lifetime and the use of recycled inputs through product design. Strengthening resource circularity also brings climate benets because reduced reliance on primary materials lowers related upstream emissions.Resource inows and outows are not considered a nancially material risk for Ericsson today, based on the latest materiality assessment. However, the long-term availability of certain metals and minerals remains important to monitor, since global demand may affect sourcing conditions and supply-chain resilience. Ongoing oversight of these dependencies supports efforts to ease pressure on nite resources and helps maintain stable access to materials for electronic manufacturing.WasteElectronic waste (e-waste) is one of the fastest-growing waste streams globally, and network hardware is part of this trend. Inefcient production processes combined with limited collection of end-of-life equipment contribute to negative environmental impacts, including risks of improper treatment and pollution.These actual negative impacts are current and expected to persist over the medium to long term. They occur both upstream and downstream in the value chain. Upstream, manufacturing processes generate waste during component production. Downstream, recovery and treatment of used equipment pose challenges. Ericssons take-back rates for network hardware remain low, partly because ownership lies with customers and products often retain resale value. While resale and second-hand markets can extend equipment lifetime, they may reduce traceability and limit the likelihood of proper recycling. As a result, some equipment is assumed to be recycled under substandard conditions. In its own operations, Ericsson generates relatively little waste, though unsold and scrapped inventory constitutes a notable internal waste stream, albeit smaller in scale than customer-owned end-of-life equipment.E-waste-related risks are currently not considered nancially material for Ericsson. Nevertheless, with global e-waste volumes projected to rise further, this remains an important issue to monitor. Addressing e-waste through improved collection and treatment practices supports responsible resource management, reduces environmental pressures and contributes to the long-term resilience of the electronics value chain.PoliciesEricssons Sustainability Policy sets out the Companys principles on environmental sustainability. The policy requires Ericsson to provide product take-back services to its customers as part of its extended producer responsibility, and to support them in the end-of-life management of products and solutions. In addition to the Code of Conduct for Business Partners, suppliers with signicant environmental impact such as manufacturing service providers, shipping and logistics companies and network rollout partners must meet additional environmental requirements. These suppliers are expected to apply a systematic approach to identify, manage, reduce and responsibly dispose of or recycle non-hazardous solid waste. They are also expected to conserve natural resources, including water, fossil fuels, minerals and virgin forest products, through measures such as process modications, material substitution, reuse, conservation and recycling, where feasible. sektioner.text: Ericsson does not currently measure the weight of input materials directly. Instead, estimates are based on the weight and volumes of sold products and scrapped inventory, which introduces timing discrepancies. The share of secondary materials is largely derived from global averages. Ericsson plans to rene its measurement methodologies going forward.These values are subject to high measurement uncertainty. Ericsson plans to rene its measurement methodologies going forward.In addition, suppliers should demonstrate that their design and supply-chain activities help reduce environmental impacts across the product life cycle, considering energy use, material consumption and end-of-life treatment. Further information about the Code of Conduct for Business Partners and the Sustainability Policy is provided in the section General disclosuresManagement actionsProduct design principles Ericsson applies the Design for Environment principles throughout its product design processes. Key requirements include material marking, ease of dismantling and disassembly to support maintenance and recycling, and durability for long product life as part of quality management. Banned and restricted substances lists and material declaration requirements, described in the section Pollutionguide material selection to support regulatory compliance and improve recyclability.Products returned through the e-Waste Management Program described below have historically shown high recyclability, averaging above 90% in recent years. Ericsson also works to reduce product weight and size and is assessing more sustainable material options in line with its Net Zero target, supporting more efcient resource use and contributing to circularity across the product life cycle. Refurbish, reuse and repairEricsson applies a structured approach to refurbishment and reuse within its Support Services portfolio. Shared warehouses and spare-parts solutions help limit the need for new production, and automated hardware fault analysis reduces unnecessary replacements. Ericsson also provides repair services and enables the reuse of returned equipment, which complements new product sales and supports circularity across the product life cycle.Management of e-wasteEricsson operates a global e-Waste Management Program in collaboration with third-party recyclers that are required to meet stringent environmental requirements. Through this program, customer-owned products at the end-of-life stage can be collected and recycled to help minimize environmental impact. A limited number of subsidiaries provide take-back services through collective take-back schemes, reecting the nature of their product portfolios. As equipment typically remains the property of customers, take-back volumes depend on customer use of these programs. Waste from own operationsEricsson primarily assembles parts and components from suppliers and therefore ates relatively little material waste, mainly ofce waste and residuals from production and packaging. During the year, the Company carried out targeted work to better quantify unsold inventory that is scrapped, with the aim of reducing these volumes over time. Ericsson also continued its programs that focus on waste reduction and improved waste handling in ofces and warehouses. Critical minerals Ericsson manages risks related to critical minerals, including rare earth elements, as part of its general sourcing processes to ensure continuity of supply and access to key production inputs. Because Ericsson purchases components and nished products rather than raw materials directly, its exposure to these materials is indirect and primarily occurs through its supply chain. To maintain supply continuity, suppliers are segmented by business criticality based on spend, risk, dependency and strategic importance. Ericsson manages disruption risks through multiple sourcing options, strategic buffer stocks and real-time monitoring of disruptive events. This monitoring helps identify suppliers affected by man-made or natural disruptions and supports the implementation of mitigation measures. It may also draw on supplier business continuity plans to provide greater detail into potential vulnerabilities. TargetsEricsson has not set targets for its material resource use and circularity-related impacts but continues to assess whether target setting would be appropriate as part of its management approach. The effectiveness of related policies and actions is, in part, monitored through its e-waste-related key performance indicators (KPIs) as disclosed on the next page.Resource inowsBuilding on its indirect exposure to raw materials through the supply chain, Ericsson is working to improve visibility into the material composition of purchased products and components. At present, the Company has limited supplier-specic data on the share of secondary raw materials incorporated into these Network equipment consists primarily of metals, and an analysis of the Bills of Materials for key products indicates that a typical radio is composed of approximately 58% aluminum, 10% copper, 8% iron or steel, 4% rubber and 3% silicon. The remaining share is made up of other compounds, including limited use of polymers such as polycarbonates (plastics), and less than 1% rare earth elements. Several of these materials are listed by the EU as critical raw materials. In 2025, the total weight of materials used in Ericssons network equipment was approximately 103,000 metric tons, of which an estimated 3,000 metric tons (3%) were secondary materials, including recycled or reused components. The estimate is derived from data provided by key suppliers and from global average recycling rates for the materials most frequently used in Ericssons volume products. As a result, the quality and the granularity of the data remain limited, and further improvements to the measurement methodology are planned. Resource outowsProducts and materials Primary resource outows from Ericssons production and outsourced manufacturing consist of network hardware, including radios, antennas, basebands, power modules, routers and modems, as well as site materials such as cables and batteries and associated packaging. All products designed by Ericsson follow generic product requirements and the Design for Environment principles, including considerations for repairability, as described above.There is no established industry benchmark for the average expected durability of network equipment, which means that comparisons between Ericssons hardware and that of peers are not possible. Ericssons network hardware is also not covered by any reparability rating system, as such schemes are generally designed for consumer electronics.Ericssons network equipment mainly consists of metals that are widely recyclable. Based on data from recycling of its own products, it is estimated that 96% of the materials are recyclableWasteEricssons material waste streams are the end-of-life treatment of customer-owned network equipment and the scrapping of unsold inventory of similar products. sektioner.rubrik: The EU taxonomy establishes a common framework to identify which
sektioner.text: economic activities can be considered environmentally sustainable. Ericsson has assessed its economic activities against the taxonomy to determine which are eligible and aligned under the Climate and Environmental Delegated Regulations.Assessment approach Identifying the economic activities relevant for Ericsson has required interpretation of the taxonomy and the related Delegated Regulations. Ericssons interpretation is that, for an economic activity to be considered taxonomy eligible, it must meet all three of the following criteria:Generate, or be aimed at generating, external turnover,match the description of an activity listed in one of the annexes to the Climate or Environmental Delegated Regulation andhave practically applicable technical screening criteria associated with it.Based on this interpretation, turnover, capital expenditure (Capex) and operational expenditure (Opex) from activities meeting these criteria have been included as taxonomy eligible in the KPIs presented on the next page. In addition, certain individually eligible expenditures are included as taxonomy eligible, as described below.As of 2025, Ericsson applies the recently introduced materiality thresholds in the taxonomy, under which economic activities that individually and in aggregate represent no more than 10% of turnover, Capex or Opex are not disclosed as separate items. These non-material activities are listed in a footnote to the summary table on the next page.It should be noted that only a few activities in the ICT sector are included in the Climate Delegated Regulation. While the European Commission has indicated that additional activities may be considered in the future, most of Ericssons commercial offering, including mobile networks, is currently not covered by activities listed as eligible under the Climate Delegated Regulation.Climate Delegated RegulationNo economic activities that qualify under the Climate Delegated Regulation generated material turnover, Capex or Opex during the reporting year. Environmental Delegated RegulationManufacture of electrical and electronic equipment (CE 1.2)Ericsson sells electronic equipment as part of its network solutions, including radios, antennas, basebands, power modules, routers, modems and site materials such as cables and batteries. The equipment is manufactured both at Ericssons own sites and by third-party electronics manufacturers.The technical screening criteria for assessing whether this activity makes a substantial contribution have been reviewed. The assessment is that these criteria were primarily developed for consumer electronics and are therefore often not directly applicable to network products. As is common for industrial equipment manufacturers, detailed information on how network products can be repaired or dismantled is not publicly disclosed, as doing so could create signicant competitive disadvantages. In addition, the products do not fully comply with all substance requirements specied in the criteria. However, the criteria related to extended producer responsibility for electrical and electronic equipment and batteries are assessed as being met.Work is ongoing to assess whether this activity meets the Do No Signicant Harm (DNSH) criteria under the EU taxonomy. The assessment includes evaluation of impacts by primary manufacturing facilities on water resources, nature and biodiversity, and exposure to location-specic climate-related hazards. As this work is ongoing, it is not yet possible to conclude whether all DNSH criteria are fully met.Most DNSH criteria related to pollution prevention and control are met. However, the general DNSH criteria are not yet fully met, as all products currently contain lead. The activity is assessed as meeting the DNSH criteria for climate change mitigation. The criteria related to energy-efciency ratings apply only to consumer electronics and are therefore not applicable to these products.Individually eligible expendituresMaterial expenditures related to economic activities other than those described above may be included as individually eligible Capex and Opex, provided that the activity is listed in either the Climate or Environmental Delegated Regulation and that the suppliers economic activity is taxonomy eligible and, where applicable, taxonomy aligned.Ericsson includes Acquisition and ownership of buildings (CCM 7.7) as individually eligible Capex and Opex. As assessing alignment for these activities requires detailed information on suppliers own taxonomy alignment, Ericsson is currently not able to determine to what extent identied individually eligible Capex and Opex can also be considered taxonomy aligned.Certain additional expenditures related to activities listed in the Climate Delegated Regulation are included within non-material activities, as presented in the footnote to the summary table on the next page.Minimum safeguards Minimum safeguards are considered to be in place. Information about Ericssons human rights commitments and due diligence processes is provided in the social sections, with an overview included in Appendix 3, and details on the approach to anti-bribery and corruption, tax compliance and competition law are presented in the sectionBusiness conductAccounting policiesEricssons consolidated nancial statements are prepared in accordance with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) as issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) and as endorsed by the EU. The basis of preparation is described in Note A1 to the consolidated nancial statements.Capex and Opex as used for taxonomy reporting are dened by the EU Taxonomy Regulation and are not standalone measures dened under IFRS. The taxonomys KPIs are calculated using amounts derived from Ericssons nancial statements and are mapped to the relevant line items. For Opex, the EU Taxonomy Regulation applies a narrowly dened cost base, which represents only a subset of operating expenses recognized in the nancial statements.Turnover Total turnover corresponds to net sales as presented in the consolidated income statement.Capex Total Capex corresponds to additions to the balance sheet items property, plant and equipment and intangible assets, including capitalized research and development costs. These amounts are reported before any remeasurement, depreciation, amortization or impairment and exclude changes in fair value. Additions arising from business combinations are included, as specied in Notes C1 and C2 to the consolidated balance sheet.EU taxonomy for sustainable activitiesEricsson 2025Board of Directors Report  Sustainability StatementFinancial ReportCorporate Governance ReportRemuneration Report- -                - -   - -     - - - - - - - -   - - -   -     .     - - E   117

By providing employees with access to learning and development in these areas, Ericsson supports their long-term employability, career growth and professional development. At the same time, strengthening these capabilities within the workforce enables Ericsson to maintain its technology leadership in mobile networks, where these skills are increasingly important. Providing employees with opportunities to build the right skills is critical not only for developing innovative solutions, but also for effectively bringing them to market and -

sektioner.text: with business priorities contributes to a workforce that is better prepared for industry transformations while supporting Ericssons ability to deliver competitive, high-quality solutions to its customers and partners. This impact is current and expected to persist over the medium to long term.Alongside these positive impacts, Ericsson has identied the disproportionately lower representation of women as an actual negative impact across the information and communications technology (ICT) sector including within its own workforce. sektioner.rubrik: Sektion 197
sektioner.text: Substandard working conditionsEricsson has employees in more than 100 countries and operates its own manufacturing and logistics sites across Europe, Asia and the Americas, which connects the Company to potential negative impacts on working conditions across its value chain. These issues are systemic in nature and are typically more prevalent upstream in the electronics manufacturing supply chain. Ericssons own exposure primarily relates to employees in manufacturing and logistics roles in higher-risk geographies, including parts of Latin America, South and Southeast Asia and China. Within Ericssons own operations in these locations, the risk of excessive working hours, inadequate pay, insecure employment, harassment, and restrictions on freedom of association and collective bargaining is assessed as heightened.Ericsson monitors working conditions across its operations worldwide through - - - -

sektioner.rubrik: Sektion 198
sektioner.text: ongoing engagement and due diligence activities. The underlying conditions giving rise to these impacts are current and expected to persist over the medium to long term. Work-related accidents and fatalities Work-related accidents occur in Ericssons own operations and, to a greater extent, among supplier personnel engaged in network rollout, maintenance and repair, where fatalities also have occurred. This actual negative impact is current and expected to persist over the medium and long term. It is concentrated in eld operations and supplier relationships across multiple regions.Based on past incident data, fatalities have resulted from road trafc accidents, falls from heights and electrocution among supplier personnel working on network sites. Lost workday incidents have mainly arisen from similar causes, as well as during assembly, disassembly and other eld-based technical activities. These impacts are linked to Ericssons business model, which involves -

sektioner.rubrik: Sektion 199
sektioner.text: large-scale network deployment and maintenance carried out both by Ericsson and its suppliers. Ericssons Target Zero goal integrates health and safety aspects into the Companys overall strategy, aiming to eliminate fatalities and lost workday accidents across Ericssons own operations and its value chain.Security of workers in high-risk areasEricsson has employees and works with suppliers in regions where conict, political instability, civil unrest or organized crime create heightened security concerns. In such contexts, workers in both Ericssons own operations and its value chain may face threats to their safety and well-being, including assault, abduction or other forms of violence.The exposure to such risks is particularly relevant for employees and supplier personnel engaged in network rollout and mainte- - - - -

sektioner.rubrik: Sektion 200
sektioner.text: directly exposed through its own employees in these geographies and indirectly through business relationships with suppliers and subcontractors. This potential negative impact is current and expected to persist over the medium to long term.Upholding fair and safe working conditions is central to Ericssons responsible business commitments and supports resilient operations and supply chains. It also aligns with Ericssons ambition to maintain trusted relationships with customers, employees and partners, and to contribute to broader industry standards on decent work and safe employment practices.Ericsson 2025Board of Directors Report  Sustainability StatementFinancial ReportCorporate Governance ReportRemuneration Report  -     119

sektioner.rubrik: PoliciesThe Code of Business Ethics applies to Ericssons employees
sektioner.text: and to any person whose work Ericsson exercises day-to-day control over. This policy prohibits all forms of discrimination, regardless of local legislation. It recognizes the right to just, safe and favorable working conditions, freedom of association and collective bargaining, and the Companys commitment to maintaining a safe and healthy work environment. It sets out Ericssons commitment to fair and reasonable pay, which includes paying, at minimum, a living wage to its employees. It strictly prohibits slavery, exploitation, human trafcking, child labor and any form of forced or compulsory labor. Further information about the Code of Business Ethics is provided in the section General Disclosures, which also describes the main elements of Ericssons Business and Human Rights Statement. Ericssons People Policy covers all of its employees and individuals performing work for Ericsson and sets out the Companys commitment to fair and equitable treatment, equal opportunities and good working conditions without discrimination. The policy is founded on the principles that every individuals employment opportunity shall be based on openness and fairness, that pay and recognition shall reward impact and be determined by market competitiveness, fairness and transparency. The policy supports continuous learning and career development to enable employees to upskill and reskill in line with evolving business needs. Leaders are responsible for fostering an engaging work environment where employees can perform at their best, grow, feel valued and contribute to Ericssons long-term success.The Health, Safety and Wellbeing Policy covers employees and, where applicable, others affected by the Companys activities, including non-employees within Ericssons workforce and employees of suppliers. It states that Ericsson shall apply a risk-based approach to prevent, control and mitigate work-related hazards and continually improve its management of these matters. Ericsson strives to comply with customer and other applicable health and safety requirements, even when these are stricter than local law. Workplaces and processes are designed to support health, safety and well-being, supported by appropriate tools and training. Engagement and consultation with employees and other stakeholders are carried out regularly to support continuous improvement of the Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) Management System. Engagement processesEngagement with the workforce about actual and potential impacts on them takes place through several channels. Company-wide employee surveys are conducted annually to assess work experience, work environment and perceptions of leadership and strategy. Results are available at Company and unit level and can be broken down by employee groups to support targeted actions.Ericsson has established OHS committees that include managers and employees, or employee representatives where applicable. The committees meet regularly, follow up on performance and discuss and decide on actions to improve the OHS Management System and its processes. Information about health, safety and well-being targets, performance and training is available for all employees through internal channels such as the intranet and newsletters. In addition, all employees are surveyed annually about health, safety and well-being, including work-life balance. Employees are covered by collective bargaining agreements with workers unions in several countries where Ericsson operates, including countries with a large employee headcount such as Sweden, Spain, Romania, Hungary, Italy and Brazil. In these countries, unions are consulted on matters related to working conditions, according to local law.Ericsson has no global framework agreements with any global union federations but maintains dialogue with the Trade Union Network, a global union body. Ericsson has also established a European Works Council that facilitates information and consultation between management and employee representatives on signicant transnational matters affecting employees in countries within the European Economic Area (EEA). Ericsson pursues its human rights objectives through collaborations and partnerships with other organizations. These initiatives support the Companys human rights due diligence and offer additional insight into the perspectives of affected stakeholders, including its own workforce. The main external collaborations, partnerships and commitments related to human and labor rights are outlined below.Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels to raise concernsEmployees can report suspected violations of the Code of Business Ethics, including suspected cases of discrimination, harassment and other negative impacts on human and labor rights, to their manager, a managers superior, the People function or the Legal and Compliance functions. Concerns can also be reported through Ericssons Compliance Line, which is accessible online or by phone at any time and in multiple languages. Anonymous reporting is available, and reporters are not required to waive their rights to judicial remedies or sign non-disclosure agreements. To protect the integrity of the investigations, reporters are asked not to share information related to ongoing cases. Ericsson has in recent years received a consistent number of reports through its Compliance Line. Many of these concern general inquiries rather than potential misconduct or breaches of the Code of Business Ethics, laws or regulations, with only a limited share of reported concerns leading to investigations or substantiated ndings. This pattern indicates that the reporting channels are accessible, well known and trusted. Further information is provided in the section Business ConductA central reporting channel is available for employees and supplier employees to report health and safety incidents and near misses. These are handled within a dedicated process within the Companys OHS Management System.When negative impacts are identied, Ericsson seeks to provide remedy, for example by engaging with affected parties or by adapting processes to prevent similar occurrences. sektioner.rubrik: Management actionsEqual treatment and opportunities for all Equal
sektioner.text: treatment and opportunities promote diversity of thought, which enhances innovation and quality of decision-making, which underpins the Companys resilience and long-term competitiveness. Ericsson works to maintain a culture grounded in respect, fairness and transparency and to address barriers to equal treatment and opportunities among its workforce. Ericssons people and talent processes are designed to treat employees and potential talent fairly and consistently, for example by using neutral language in job postings and providing leaders with training on fostering equal treatment and opportunities.Creating an inclusive work environment and a culture of belonging is embedded in the business and is the responsibility of each manager for their team. The topic expertise resides within the Global Talent & Development organization, which is responsible for establishing frameworks and guidelines. Employee resource groups are supported and encouraged throughout the organization. These are open to all employees and cover a variety of topics. Pay and benets are designed to be fair, competitive and reective of individual performance and contribution. All pay decisions follow Ericssons pay philosophy and use the same non-discrimination criteria. A globally consistent job architecture and dened job levels provide the infrastructure to support fair pay practices and enable meaningful In 2025, Ericsson completed a comprehensive analysis of wage adequacy. The analysis conrmed that all employees receive wages assessed as adequate under the Companys applied methodology, which is aligned with ESRS requirements. Going forward, Ericsson will continuously assess the wages paid to employees, in line with its commitment to fair and reasonable pay, which includes ensuring that all employees receive at least a living wage. Employees development is supported through upskilling, reskilling, project-based learning and internal mobility. Each year, Ericsson identies critical skills linked to its strategic priorities, covering technology, business and leadership competencies. Learning opportunities to develop these skills are offered across four prociency levels to support employees in meeting performance expectations in their current roles and preparing for future career opportunities. Employees are encouraged to build connections within the Company to foster knowledge-sharing and to network across the organization. A digital learning experience platform provides access to self-paced courses and enables tracking and analysis of skills development. Employees can also nominate themselves for targeted learning programs developed with external partners and universities. Individual career development and performance goals are set annually with managers, and employees receive yearly performance evaluations to support their development. Employees can explore and apply for project assignments and rotation opportunities, in addition to open job roles, through Ericssons internal talent marketplace.In 2025, Ericsson focused on clarifying expectations on good leadership by anchoring these in three foundational principles: creating clarity, developing people and delivering results. Leaders receive support in understanding and applying these principles through targeted workshops, programs and user-friendly guidance materials. Health and safety Ericsson is committed to providing a safe and healthy work environment and its overarching goal is Target Zero, meaning zero work-related fatalities and lost workday incidents. Ericsson Care is the Companys approach to health, safety and well-being, which supports Target Zero by promoting safe and healthy behaviors across the organization. The approach is supported by programs focused on proactive risk prevention, safety leadership, supplier engagement, learning and development, and communication and awareness within Ericsson and among its suppliers. All managers are responsible for implementing these programs by fostering a safe and healthy work environment, ensuring that team members complete relevant OHS training, and promoting awareness and compliance. Ericsson has a global reporting tool for reporting hazards, near misses, incidents and remote work-related concerns involving employees, suppliers or others working on behalf of the Company. Reported incidents are investigated using root-cause analysis to address damage and prevent recurrence. All Ericsson employees and employees of site services suppliers are required to complete mandatory health, safety and well-being training. Additional training is provided based on a persons role and risk exposure, complemented by specic training for leaders and other key roles to improve the safety culture. In 2025, the Company continued to further embed safety in its culture and to strengthen processes and governance. This included launching updated mandatory training that emphasized Ericssons commitment to providing a safe and healthy work environment for all employees and anyone working on its behalf. The training was designed to create more engagement and encourages employees to take proactive and preventive action, such as reporting hazards, speaking up, responding to emergencies and prioritizing the well-being of themselves and others. Additionally, the Stop Work Authority Program continues to encourage and empower employees and supplier employees to immediately stop work when unsafe working conditions are identied. Efforts during the year related to the health and safety of eld service suppliers are detailed in Workers in the value chainWorking conditionsHuman rights due diligenceHuman rights due diligence is integrated into Ericssons business operations to support its commitment to respect human rights and to manage risks. Related risks are included in the ERM framework and are overseen by the Business Risk Committee as needed. A central team of human rights experts sets group-level priorities, coordinates due diligence and works with business areas and regional sales teams on human rights initiatives. Human rights training is made available to all employees, and targeted training and capacity building for key job roles and functions are offered. Salient human rights issues relate mainly to supply-chain workers and potential misuse of Ericssons technology in the downstream value chain. These are addressed in the Workers in the value chain Consumers and end usersFor its own operations and workforce, Ericsson applies a range of human rights due diligence measures in relation to activities or operations where risks are assessed to be elevated, in line with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises. One such measure is the use of country visits and studies aimed at gaining a deeper understanding of local contexts and potential human rights impacts. In recent years, human rights experts have conducted visits to operations in Mexico and India, engaging in dialogues with local employees and management, visiting suppliers and organizing meetings and roundtables with civil society organizations focusing on human rights issues of concern to Ericsson. The main outcomes of these visits have been an increased understanding of country-specic operations and related risks, increased awareness of human rights due diligence and identication of potential negative impacts and actions to address them. Human rights considerations are also included in Ericssons due diligence process related to mergers, acquisitions and divestitures. sektioner.rubrik: The Code of Conduct for Business Partners requires business partners,
sektioner.text: such as suppliers, to respect all internationally recognized human rights standards, including the International Bill of Human Rights and International Labor Organization (ILO). Business partners must: provide clear, written employment agreements, ensure employees do not pay recruitment fees and allow migrant workers access to identication or immigration documents. Forced, bonded and child labor are prohibited. Young employees under the age of 18 must not perform work that is likely to jeopardize their health or safety, including night shifts and overtime. Working hours must comply with local laws, not exceed 60 hours per week including overtime, and should strive toward the ILO standard of 48 hours per week. Employees must earn a living wage that meets basic needs and allows for some discretionary income. Workplaces must be free from unlawful discrimination, harassment or inhumane treatment, and employees should have the right to form unions and engage in collective bargaining.Ericsson offers free training on the Code of Conduct to its suppliers. In addition, targeted content covering anti-corruption, human rights, conict minerals and OHS is available on the Companys website, which also provides access to the United Nations Global Compact Academy for employees in Ericssons sourcing organization.The Code requires business partners to implement a risk-based approach to health and safety, provide relevant training, and maintain incident reporting and corrective action processes. They are also required to have an OHS management system. Specic OHS standards apply to suppliers involved in construction, eld maintenance and network rollout, including requirements for managing subcontractors.Further information on the Code of Conduct for Business Partners is provided in the General disclosureswhich also describes the main elements of Ericssons Business and Human Rights Statement.Engagement processesEricsson uses direct and indirect channels to engage with workers in its value chain on actual and potential impacts affecting them. The Code of Conduct Audit Program, which targets suppliers, includes worker interviews focused on human and labor rights and is described below. Ericsson regularly engages with organizations as proxies for the views of workers in the value chain. This includes membership in the Shift Business Learning Program to promote business respect for human rights according to the United Nations Guiding Principles for Business and Human Rights (UNGPs), the Business Network on Civic Freedoms and Human Rights Defenders, and the Responsible Business Alliance (RBA). Heightened due diligence activities involve direct engagement with labor rights organizations and roundtables with civil society and other stakeholders as relevant. Ericsson is working closely with the Responsible Minerals Initiative (RMI) and participates in its working groups, where it chairs the Aluminum Working Group.Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels to raise concernsFindings from supplier audits are addressed through time-bound corrective action plans, making them a key mechanism for remediating negative impacts on value-chain workers. Workers can report concerns about violations of the Code of Conduct for Business Partners, policies, laws or regulation through the Ericsson Compliance Line, which is available to internal and external stakeholders, including suppliers and their employees (see Business conduct. Business partners must maintain their own grievance mechanisms that enable employees to raise concerns safely and without fear of reprisal or retaliation.In 2025, no severe negative human rights impacts related to workers in the value chain were reported through Ericssons channels, and no remediation actions were therefore undertaken.Management actionsEricsson is committed to conducting business responsibly and has established several processes to manage impacts on workers in its value chain. The key actions described below relate to: supplier screening and auditing, critical minerals and supply-chain traceability, and supplier health and safety management. Supplier screening and auditingA dedicated unit within Ericssons sourcing organization drives sustainability and corporate responsibility initiatives, focusing on supplier compliance with the Code of Conduct for Business Partners via risk assessments and dedicated Code of Conduct audits. Suppliers must agree to the Code of Conduct before entering into business with Ericsson, and rst-tier suppliers are assessed for risks of nonconformity regarding its provisions. New suppliers are screened and selected based on multiple criteria, including environmental and social factors, using third-party databases to identify instances of adverse media, instances of regulatory non-compliance, anticompetitive behavior, nancial irregularities, as well as environment, production, and labor and human-rights issues.A modular supplier-sustainability risk assessment may be activated depending on the suppliers risk prole, with the scope determined by the type of products or services provided. When a supplier is selected for assessment, relevant self-assessment questionnaires covering environmental, health and safety and human-rights management topics are sent for completion.Following the assessment, suppliers receive a risk rating, and based on the outcome, a recommendation is made to approve, not approve, or approve the supplier with specic conditions to address identied gaps (or the equivalent recommendations for active suppliers). Once onboarded, suppliers are continuously screened for adverse media coverage at regular intervals. When initial screenings or assessments identify potentially elevated human-rights risks, Ericsson conducts heightened human-rights due diligence to further evaluate and address these risks. The process may include desktop studies of the security and regulatory environment, forced-labor screenings using third-party risk data providers, and engagement with peers through channels such as the Responsible Business Alliance or Responsible Minerals Initiative. Ericsson may also consult civil-society organizations or other external stakeholders to better understand local contexts. Where heightened risks are conrmed, Ericsson works with rst-tier suppliers to reinforce Code of Conduct requirements and may require external audits and time-bound corrective action plans. The human rights-focused country visits described in the section Own workforce also covered matters related to workers in the value chain.Ericsson audits its rst-tier suppliers to verify compliance with the Code of Conduct. These audits focus on suppliers identied as having heightened environmental, human-rights, labor or business-conduct-related risks. In scope for selection are primarily suppliers that fall within the top 90% total procurement spend. Supplier risk, determined by factors such as country, product or service type, time since last audit and purchase volume, guides the audit selection process. Audits are conducted by an external provider, mainly on-site, with remote audits used for high-risk countries or follow-ups. Focus areas include employment conditions, working hours, wages, health and safety, chemical handling and the suppliers communication of requirements to their own suppliers.Nonconformities must be resolved through time-bound corrective action plans. Audits are not conducted on an unannounced basis, but semi-announced audits are carried out, where suppliers are informed that an audit will occur within a dened time frame without disclosure of the exact date and time.Ericsson 2025Board of Directors Report  Sustainability StatementFinancial ReportCorporate Governance ReportRemuneration Report- - - section     ,  - - - - the section     )   - - -   - - -   - - - - -       126

Its exposure to raw materials, including conict minerals, is indirect, through the materials and minerals used in components forming part of the electronic hardware sold in network solutions. This indirect exposure makes thorough due diligence and industry collaboration essential to managing related risks.Ericsson is committed to sourcing critical minerals, including tantalum, tungsten, lithium and nickel, in compliance with all applicable legislation. The Companys due diligence measures align with the OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible Supply Chains of Minerals and comply with emerging regulations such as the EU Battery Regulation and the Critical Raw Materials Act.Suppliers of electronic hardware are required to conduct due diligence on the sourcing and extraction of critical minerals and to verify, with reasonable certainty, the origin of minerals in products supplied to Ericsson. Traceability beyond rst-tier suppliers is pursued primarily via engagement in industry networks and associations, using tools and templates of the RMI to map supply chains and identify smelters and reners. Ericsson also uses RMI assessment data on identied smelters and reners to determine whether enhanced due diligence or supplier collaboration is warranted.Ericsson seeks to increase sourcing from suppliers and sub-suppliers that meet relevant minerals-sustainability standards, such as those of the RMI. The Company uses the RMI framework, working groups and tools to engage directly with smelters where no direct business relationship exists, or to strengthen requirements on sub-suppliers through direct suppliers. Ericsson strives to work collaboratively with suppliers toward continuous improvement but may terminate business relationships as a last resort in case of recurring noncompliance.Further details are provided in Ericssons annual Conict Minerals Report on Form SD, published on its website and led with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.Supplier health and safety management Ericsson has established global requirements for eld service suppliers as part of its Code of Conduct for Business Partners. Key requirements are incident reporting and investigation, hazard and risk management, communication and awareness, Stop Work Authority and mandatory training. The Stop Work Authority requires and empowers personnel to immediately stop work when unsafe conditions are identied. Through supplier safety maturity assessments, Ericsson evaluates site service suppliers against predened health and safety criteria. Based on the results, improvement plans must be completed within set time-frames, and new suppliers must successfully complete the assessment before onboarding. For active suppliers, follow-up assessments aim to drive improvement in safety performance. Suppliers must complete mandatory training courses dened by Ericsson, including health and safety induction, safe driving awareness and lifesaving rules. Consequence management applies when suppliers fail to close actions within agreed time frames, decline to participate in assessments or breach Ericssons safety requirements. Possible measures include nancial penalties, reduced business volumes, additional inspections or audits, written warnings or, in severe cases, termination of the supplier relationship. Health and safety measures Own workforcealso apply to site service supplier employees.In 2025, Ericsson continued to conduct Target Zero workshops to strengthen safety culture across its supply base, and implemented a Supplier Safety Recognition Program to further promote safe behavior. Under this program, suppliers were recognized locally and globally in three categories: safe behavior, best practice and top improvement suggestion. Maturity assessments for site-service suppliers continued in 2025, focusing on improving safety maturity and evaluating new suppliers.TargetsEricsson has a target for zero fatalities and lost-workday incidents, which covers both its own workforce and employees of site service suppliers. Independent research indicates that higher levels of mobile broadband adoption are associated with increased economic growth, particularly in low-income countries, and that improved school connectivity can support long-term social and economic benets. Mobile networks also facilitate nancial inclusion, as many people without access to traditional banking services already own mobile phones that can provide access to mobile nancial services.Despite this potential, an estimated one-third of the global population still lacks access to reliable mobile broadband. The connectivity gap has two main dimensions. Some people live outside network coverage, while others are covered but face barriers such as insufcient connection quality, affordability constraints, limited digital skills or challenges using available services. Addressing these gaps generally requires new business models and policies to expand infrastructure, making access more affordable and broadening digital skills development. Ericsson contributes through solutions such as Fixed Wireless Access and through initiatives like Connect To Learn, which support digital literacy and school connectivity.These societal-level systemic impacts are linked to Ericssons business model and strategy, as the Company provides mobile network infrastructure that enables digitalization. The impact is actual, positive and occurs downstream during the use phase of mobile networks, particularly in regions with low or uneven broadband penetration. It is current and expected to persist over the medium to long term, with benets arising as coverage improves and broader socioeconomic effects developing over time. Ericsson contributes through technology development and deployment, and through business relationships with customers and partners that operate and expand the networks.Information on negative impacts on communities related to the sourcing of minerals from conict-affected and high-risk areas is provided in the sectionWorkers in the value chainPoliciesEricsson has a long history in technology development and considers access to communications to be an essential need. The Company is committed to support global access to communications. The Code of Business Ethics states that support to local communities should aim to create a positive impact. Activities are assessed to ensure alignment with strategy and to conrm that resources are used responsibly. Due diligence is carried out to avoid conicts of interest or links to improper payments. Further information on the Code of Business Ethics is provided in General disclosureswhich also describes the main elements of Ericssons Business and Human Rights Statement.Engagement processesDirect engagement with affected communities takes place occasionally, but most interaction occurs through organizations, partnerships and key memberships, which are outlined below. In addition, Ericssons membership in the Global Network Initiative focuses on issues related to the responsible use of technology. Further information is provided in the Consumers and end usersOrganizationITU (International Telecommunication Union)Ericsson partners with the ITU on initiatives to address challenges related to digital infrastructure gaps, universal school connectivity and digital transformation. The collaboration includes developing tools and training to support policymakers in improving sustainable connectivity in underserved areas and communities.ITU/UNESCO Broadband Commission for Sustainable DevelopmentEricssons CTO serves as a Commissioner on the Broadband Commission for Sustainable Development, a multi-stakeholder, high-level platform that develops policy recommendations on universal meaningful connectivity and the role of broadband in global sustainable development. A substantial share of recent 5G Fixed Wireless Access launches has been in emerging markets. Ericssons digital inclusion activities also include education and digital skills development through Connect To Learn, a program delivered in partnership with governments, service providers, NGOs and UN agencies. Connect To Learn supports digital connectivity for schools and community learning centers and provides training that strengthens students digital skills and chances for future employment. The program includes two main offerings: Ericsson Educate: An e-learning platform that offers university-level training in telecommunications and emerging technologies, such as 5G, AI, data science, automation and IoT.Ericsson Digital Lab: Project-based activities designed for learners aged 1116 that introduce fundamental concepts in areas such as coding, robotics, game development, electronics and AI.Since 2022, Ericsson has contributed to the Digital Transformation Collaborative led by UNESCO under the Global Education Coalition. The initiative provides governments with tools and guidance to integrate digital education into national planning and to build capacity through training and workshops.Ericsson and the International Telecommunication Union are co-developing the Connectivity Planning Platform, a tool that helps map ICT infrastructure, identify underserved areas and assess connectivity solutions. The platform is intended to support evidence-based planning and investment decisions aimed at expanding affordable and resilient connectivity.Financial inclusion Ericssons Mobile Wallet Platform supports communications service providers and nancial institutions in offering mobile-based nancial services. sektioner.text: subtopicImpact, risk or opportunityTypeImpact occursFinancial driverInformation-related impacts for end usersMisuse of technology Potential negative impactDownstreamData breaches and infrastructure Potential negative impactDownstreamNetwork security (entity-specific reporting subtopic)Inadequate network security measuresLoss of businessMisuse of technologyEricssons technologies are designed to provide secure and reliable connectivity, but they may also be used in ways that could negatively affect consumers and end users depending on the context and actors involved. Potential negative impacts include breaches of privacy rights, for example through surveillance of private communications, and restrictions on freedom of expression, such as the blocking or ltering of online content.These impacts can arise when network features, such as performance management functions, are used beyond their intended legitimate purpose, including by authorities. In some contexts, Ericsson may also be indirectly required to support temporary network shutdowns when operating networks on behalf of customers. Ericsson does not receive such requests directly, but misuse downstream can still affect the rights of people who depend on the networks.These impacts are not limited to specic groups of end users. Their likelihood and severity depend on the broader context, including the strength of human rights protections, legal and regulatory frameworks, rule of law and democratic institutions in the countries where the technologies are deployed. They are current and expected to persist over the medium to long term.Like network security, preventing the misuse of technology supports trust in digital infrastructure. Ericssons approach includes human rights due diligence, contractual safeguards, technical mitigations and stakeholder engagement to help identify risks of misuse and support responsible use of its technologies.Network securityEricssons networks carry an estimated 50% of global mobile 5G trafc outside China, making their security and reliability critical for consumers and end users worldwide. These networks handle sensitive personal data and support essential services such as health care, utilities and public safety. Therefore, a data breach or disruption can result in negative effects on individuals and society. These are potential negative impacts that are current and likely to persist over the medium to long term.These impacts are linked to Ericssons role in delivering critical connectivity infrastructure. Ensuring robust security safeguards is therefore central to maintaining customer condence and supporting secure and reliable networks. No specic vulnerable groups have been identied, as these issues affect all types of end users due to the widespread reliance on connectivity.Failures in network security, such as unplanned outages or the exposure of sensitive data, can result in reputational harm, contractual issues or deployment delays. In severe cases, they may lead to loss of business, making network security a nancially material risk as well as a consumer and end-user impact. This risk is current and expected to persist over the medium to long term. Addressing these concerns is an integral part of Ericssons strategy and is embedded in its approach to supporting resilience in critical infrastructure.PoliciesThe Code of Business Ethics outlines Ericssons commitment to respect freedom of expression and privacy and requires the mitigation of risks related to the misuse of technology. Employees must assess external requests that may affect these rights and verify that such requests are legitimate, proportionate and necessary before responding. Internal procedures to mitigate associated risks must be followed, and concerns must be raised if risks are overlooked or insufciently addressed. Ericsson is a member of the Global Network Initiative (GNI) and adheres to its Principles on Freedom of Expression and Privacy. Further information about the Code of Business Ethics is provided in the section General disclosureswhich also describes the main elements of Ericssons Business and Human Rights Statement. The Development, Innovation and Use of Technology Policy sets out Ericssons commitment to the responsible, compliant and ethical use of technology. It provides guidance across the design, development, sale, deployment and use of Ericssons products and aims to ensure that technology-related decisions are appropriately considered and that potential risks, including ethical and human rights risks, are identied, assessed and addressed.Ericsson maintains a Company-wide security policy that aims to prevent, detect, respond to, remediate data and recover from breaches and infrastructure disruption that affect its networks and services. Further information is provided in the subsection Security policy on page 20 of the Board of Directors report.Engagement processesIn general, Ericsson does not engage directly with consumers and end users on potential impacts, as it does not have a direct relationship with these stakeholders. Instead, input is obtained through organizations such as the GNI and its members, which act as credible proxy stakeholders. The GNI brings together participants from academia, civil society, business and investors to set standards for responsible decision-making on freedom of expression and privacy in the ICT sector. Membership involves engagement with civil society to better understand potential human rights impacts, participation in shared learning and collective advocacy, and periodic independent assessments of company practices against the GNI Principles.Ericsson also uses its membership in the Business Network on Civic Freedoms and Human Rights Defenders to discuss and assess human-rights-related risks, including surveillance concerns, mitigation measures and relevant business activities. These engagements are conducted in ways that consider stakeholder safety.Ericsson has not yet prepared disclosures fully in accordance with ESRS S4 (Consumers and end users), but provides information in respect of this standard that is broadly aligned with its disclosure requirements. Sensitive Business processHuman rights due diligence is integrated into the sales process and other business engagements through the Sensitive Business process to help prevent and mitigate potential misuse of Ericssons technology. All sales opportunities are screened against predened human-rights-related parameters. Identied risks are assessed by a team of specialists using Ericssons Sensitive Business risk methodology, which focuses on the right to privacy, freedom of expression and related human rights. Four main parameters are considered in the Sensitive Business process. PortfolioPurposeThe amount and type of personally identiable information that may be processed, and how it will be accessed and stored.The customers intended use of the product, service or solution, and the context in which it will be operated.CustomerCountryThe nature of the customer and its ownership structure.The human rights risk prole of the country, including factors related to privacy, freedom of expression, security and conict and the rule of law.Depending on the level of identied risk, recommendations are issued on whether to proceed, proceed with mitigating measures or not pursue the opportunity. Particularly sensitive cases may be escalated to Ericssons Business Risk Committee for further review. The process also includes mechanisms to monitor adherence to issued recommendations to support effective risk management.Each regional sales organization has a designated contact person for Sensitive Business who keeps account managers and other relevant stakeholders informed about updates, information requests and related matters. The Sensitive Business process also applies to other business engagements, including mergers and acquisitions and assessments of third parties such as business and technology partners. Depending on the risk level, it may trigger actions such as legal reviews or heightened human rights due diligence before any transaction proceeds.In 2025, Ericsson strengthened awareness and capabilities across key employee groups through training and information sessions. The Sensitive Business Framework was enhanced through the introduction of a dedicated channel for analyzing and reporting requests for activities carried out on a network that may have negative impacts on human rights.
