sektioner.rubrik: Introduction and key 2025 governance updatesTo be an industry
sektioner.text: leader, technology leadership needs to be combined with operational excellence, including in how Ericsson conducts its business. Ericsson believes that strong corporate governance leads to better tiveness, improving its ability to effectively execute on its strategy and, ultimately, driving shareholder value.Ericssons corporate governanceEricsson is committed to maintaining the highest standards of corporate governance and has established a corporate governance framework that:Empowers the business, enabling strategic execution and operational excellence.Promotes and facilitates effective oversight across the organization by the Board of Directors (the Board), the President and CEO, and the Executive Team, throughout all levels of the organization. Facilitates high-quality decision-making with clear accountabilities at all levels.Instills a robust approach to risk management to effectively identify, consider, manage and mitigate risks and capture opportunities.Drives simplification, facilitating the organizational drive to improve ways of working and clear up processes that are no longer fit for their intended purpose nor underpin strong execution.Key corporate governance actions in 2025Ericsson continued its intensive work on strengthening and simplifying its corporate governance practices throughout 2025, including solidifying and clarifying the top tier of Group governance through a set of core governance pillars. Governance pillarsThe governance pillars were established to further embed an improved and clear, based governance framework that guides its people while building on their strengths  fostering a culture of transparency, collaboration and open dialogue, sound and ethical business decisions, strong risk management, clear and consistent remediation of misconduct, and cross-functional coordination. Throughout 2025, Ericsson focused on rening the structure of its steering documents and solidied the core governance pillars framework, consisting of a set of core Group principles, protocols and policies, as the top tier of Group governance steering documents. These governance pillars are the cornerstone of Ericssons governance framework and form the foundation of the Groups operations. The governance pillars set principles and requirements to guide and empower high-quality decision-making, strong oversight, improved risk management and simplication across the Group and articulate the core rules, expectations and relevant standards (both internal and external) for Ericsson and its employees, while enabling cross-functional coordination and collaboration.House of Policies Comprised of all Group-wide policies, the House of Policies establishes the requirements and expectations on the relevant topics covered by each policy and together, they comprise the essential rules of the road for conduct across the Group, articulating the core principles necessary to operate Ericsson's business and satisfy its internal standards and relevant external standards. During 2025, Ericsson continued to simplify, refresh and develop the House of Policies to establish policies that are streamlined, relevant and designed to be universally applicable across the Group. For example, in 2025, Ericsson established the:Development, Innovation and Use of Technology Group Policy which clarifies the principles for decision-making regarding the design, development, sale, deployment and use of Ericssons products and the framework and governance for implementing these principles; andArtificial Intelligence Group Directivewhich is designed to accelerate the adoption of AI technology within Ericsson in a responsible and trustworthy manner in alignment with its values and good governance.Group Decision-Making Protocol: Clarifies decision-making authority and accountability, providing an effective and cohesive framework to promote collaboration and cross-functional coordination and help ensure key matters are escalated appropriately, while also empowering its people and facilitating simplification and decision-making agility.Priority Group Contract Protocol Clarifies accountabilities, ownership and oversight regarding the most important Group contracts and successfully implemented the Priority Group Contract Committee to provide rigor in relation to the most important contracts.Material Group Risk Protocol Sets out clear requirements for identifying and escalating material group risks within Ericsson. During 2025, Ericsson continued to leverage the successful implementation of the Material Group Risk Protocol and Business Risk Committee into the Groups governance and risk management frameworks to support effective risk identification, mitigation and monitoring.Ericssons core valuesProfessionalismPerseveranceRespectIntegrityEricssons core valuesThe Companys core values are the touchstones of its culture. They guide employees daily work, in how they relate to each other and the world around them and in the way the Company does business. As Ericssonexecutes its strategy, people are the foundation, embracing and carrying forward Ericssons core values of professionalism, perseverance, respect and integrity. At Ericsson, the satisfaction and well-being of employees is both consistent with its core values and a key element of its ability to compete and succeed in the future.High quality decision-making and good risk management in a highly complex and competitive global environment require a highly capable workforce with a broad range and diversity of perspectives. At Ericsson, we cultivate an inclusive environment where everyone belongs and feels supported. Our decisions are inclusive and merit-based, and we foster a culture built on respect and professionalism. Fostering an inclusive environment is critical, as we know that when our people feel safe being themselves and they know they have the freedom and empowerment to make decisions, they will be more productive and innovative. These efforts enhance decision-making and productivity, transform how Ericsson works, and enable faster, smarter outcomes  building capabilities for today while preparing for future opportunities. Ericsson plans to use carbon removal technologies to neutralize the unavoidable part of value-chain emissions to reach its 2040 Net Zero targets.Internal carbon pricingEricsson currently does not apply an internal carbon price that results in internal transfer of funds or that is used when preparing Þnancial statements.GHG accounting methodologyEmissions are reported in accordance with the GHG Protocol, using the same consolidation approach as for the Þnancial statements. If Ericsson were to gain operational control over a non-consolidated entity or asset, related Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions would be included based on operational control rather than equity share. No such arrangements existed during the reporting year, and operational boundaries remained unchanged from the previous period.Emission calculations are based on the latest available data at the cut-off date, supplemented with extrapolated estimates for periods without measured data. Emissions are reported in COe and include carbon dioxide (CO), methane (CH), nitrous oxide O), hydroßuorocarbons (HFCs), perßuorochemicals (PFCs), sulfur hexaßuoride (SFand nitrogen trißuoride (NF). The most signiÞcant emission factors applied are listed in Appendix 4.Scope 1 Consumed volumes of fuels and refrigerants are multiplied by applicable emission factors to derive emissions. Fuel consumption in the service-vehicle ßeet is calculated using a combination of telematics data and internal estimates. For leased vehicles lacking telematics, consumption is estimated from contracted annual mileage and internal assessments of driven distances. Scope 2Purchased-energy volumes are converted to emissions using country-speciÞc average factors for location-based calculations. For market-based emissions, factors are derived from the residual energy mix and purchased renewable-energy instruments. Further details are provided in the subsection Energy consumption and mix in own operations.Scope 3Emission factors for the categories Capital goods, Fuel- and energy-related activities, Waste generated in operations, and End-of-life treatment of sold products are largely based on internal studies and EricssonÕs life-cycle assessment of product carbon footprints, multiplied by relevant activity metrics to estimate annual emissions.Emissions in the Purchased goods and services category are estimated using cradle-to-gate emissions calculated per product, based on material composition and supplier-speciÞc emission factors from primary and secondary data sources. Per-unit cradle-to-gate emissions are multiplied by the number of delivered units. This category also includes emissions from externally purchased cloud-storage and processing capacity.Upstream transportation emissions are estimated using a mix of spend-based data and calculations derived from shipment weights and distances paid for by Ericsson. Business travel emissions are calculated primarily from ßight route, distance and ticket-class data, with hotel nights estimated from travel spend. Employee commuting emissions are based on surveys of employeesÕ commuting and teleworking habits.Lifetime product emissions in the Use of sold products category are estimated and reported in full in the year the products are sold, assuming an average product lifetime of 10 years. Life-cycle grid-emission factors for the use phase are estimated from the current energy mix of markets served, or from customer-speciÞc energy-mix data when publicly available. Future changes in grid factors or customer energy mixes are not reßected.Downstream transportation emissions are mainly calculated from shipment weights and distances where transport is paid for by the customer. The remaining Scope 3 categories have been assessed as not material and are therefore not reported.The reported Þgures are subject to uncertainty due to data limitations and should be regarded as estimates rather than precise values. sektioner.text: reductions via digitalizationActual positive Digital solutions enabled by EricssonÕs networks can help reduce energy consumption and GHG emissions across multiple industries. By using ICT-solutions to optimize processes like manufacturing and maintenance, these solutions support efÞciency gains that enable industries to lower their environmental impact.GHG emissions in the value Actual negative Mobile networks consume signiÞcant energy when in use, leading to GHG emissions that account for around 90% of EricssonÕs total value-chain carbon footprint. The production of network hardware, including materials, manufacturing and transport, generates another 8 to 9% of value-chain emissions. Emissions from EricssonÕs own operations are comparatively small, but remain relevant to address as part of reducing total value-chain emissions. Network energy performanceRisk / opportunityCustomer demand for products and Energy is a signiÞcant cost component for communications service providers, and network energy performance inßuences their purchasing decisions. EricssonÕs ability to improve the energy efÞciency of its portfolio represents both a risk and an opportunity, as it may affect customer demand, market share and revenue development.PollutionTypeImpact occursFinancial driverSubstances used in electronics manufacturingSystemic negative Ericsson does not add hazardous substances in its own assembly processes, but electronics generally contain small amounts of substances of concern introduced during component manufacturing. If not properly managed or disposed of, these substances can leak into the environment and pose risk of harm to ecosystems and human health.Water and marine resourcesTypeImpact occursFinancial driverWater used in electronics manufacturing Systemic negative Ericsson does not use water in its assembly processes, but large volumes are consumed upstream in the value chain, particularly in mineral extraction and semiconductor manufacturing, which requires ultra-pure water. Poor water management at these stages can reduce the availability and quality of freshwater at source locations.Resource use and circularityTypeImpact occursFinancial driverMetals and minerals used in electronics manufacturingActual negative Network hardware production relies on metals and minerals such as iron, aluminum, copper and other critical raw materials. Without effective reuse and recycling practices, this reliance contributes to the demand for primary raw material extraction, leading to increased pressures on Þnite natural resources.Generation of electronic wasteActual negative Waste is generated across the value chain, in particular during production and through the treatment of end-of-life equipment. E-waste is one of the fastest-growing waste streams globally, and collection of end-of-life hardware is challenging because resale and secondary markets can reduce traceability and limit the likelihood of proper recycling.
